title: Struct Pointers (->)
concept: The convenient arrow operator for accessing struct members through a pointer

steps.title: Include stdio.h header
steps.explanation:
This header is for using `printf`.

This lesson covers how to pass a struct by pointer to modify the original.

steps.title: Define Player struct
steps.explanation:
`Player` is a struct type that bundles a name and health points.

It serves as the basic unit for treating related data as a single object.

steps.title: Define heal function (uses pointer)
steps.explanation:
`heal(struct Player *p)` receives the address of a Player struct.

Receiving the address allows the function to directly modify the original's members.

steps.title: Start main function
steps.explanation: The main frame is created, preparing a player instance.

steps.title: Create struct variable
steps.explanation:
We set the initial name and health for the `warrior` variable.

This value becomes the baseline state before the function call.

steps.title: Print initial health
steps.explanation: We print the health before the call to record the pre-change state.

steps.title: Call heal function (pass address)
steps.explanation:
We pass the struct's address with `heal(&warrior)`.

Instead of a copy, we pass the original's location so modifications are reflected.

steps.title: Method 1: Dereference then dot operator
steps.explanation: We can access a member with `(*p).hp` by dereferencing first, then using the dot operator.

steps.title: Method 2: Arrow operator (->)
steps.explanation:
`p->hp` is shorthand for `(*p).hp` -- they mean the same thing.

The arrow notation is the standard way to access members through a pointer.

steps.title: Verify changed health
steps.explanation:
Checking the health after the function call shows the original value was actually modified.

This demonstrates that passing by pointer leads to modification of the original.

steps.title: Program terminates
steps.explanation:
The program exits with `return 0;`.

Key point: when passing a struct pointer, use `->` for member access.

quiz.question: Given struct A *ptr; what is the correct way to access member x?
quiz.explanation:
Since it is a pointer, you must use the arrow (`->`).
`ptr.x` is only used when ptr is a struct variable.
`*ptr.x` becomes `*(ptr.x)` due to operator precedence, which is incorrect syntax.

misconceptions.correct: It is a fundamental C language feature.
misconceptions.why: It was created as a shortcut because struct pointer access is so common.

keyTakeaway: For struct pointers, use `->` instead of `.`.
